fonts.text: Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.
Sow
Feb – Mar
Harvest
Jul – Oct
Germination
8–11 days
Yield per plant
8 lb
Ready in
About 16 weeks from sowing
Bright: usual months · Muted: less usual
Cherry And Small Fruited
A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.
Ordinary
A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.
F1 Hybrid
An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.
Cherry And Small Fruited
A cordon tomato producing many small red cherry fruits. Complements orange Sungold with a familiar red-fruited alternative.
Novelty
A plum tomato for sauces and cooking. Give it warm protected conditions and distinguish it from fresh-eating cherry selections.
Tomato blight causes brown lesions on leaves and stems, followed by fruit decay and plant collapse in favourable damp conditions.
Whitefly adults and immature stages suck sap; sticky honeydew can support black sooty mould.
A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.
Irregular watering, particularly soaking after severe drying, can split ripe fruit.
Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.
Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.
Use fertile, well-drained border soil enriched with compost, or suitable pots and growing bags with fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding attention than a well-prepared border.
Sow in trays or small pots. Keep compost moist, not wet; prick out and pot on as needed. Bright light gives stout seedlings.
Once the greenhouse is warm, plant well-rooted plants in pots, growbags or beds. Water first, set slightly deeper and support cordons with canes or string.

Pots / growbags One plant per 12–18 in. diameter pot; two per standard growbag. Use peat-free compost.Pot spacing Upright cordons: about 24 in. between pot centres for foliage space.Soil beds Plants 18–24 in. apart in compost-enriched soil; wider for vigorous cordons and airflow.
For unheated cover, sow around March in gentle warmth near 68°F. Earlier heated-house crops need reliable warmth and bright light through winter.

Tie cordons loosely and remove young side shoots; take yellow lower leaves sparingly. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Bush and semi-determinate types need their own pruning regime.

Water roots steadily; feed organically at the product rate as fruit develops. Ventilate in heat and tap flowering trusses gently. Adjust autumn watering to growth; dry-to-wet swings encourage splitting and blossom-end rot.

Pick fully coloured fruit gently; use promptly. Before cold ends the crop, bring sound unripe fruit indoors. Ripen at room temperature, checking trays for decay; a nearby ripe apple or banana can help.
Problem
What to look for
What to do
BLIGHT
Brown leaf lesions; fruit may rot.
Remove infected plants; keep leaves dry and ventilate.
Greenhouse Whitefly
White flies, sticky leaves and sooty mould.
Identify early; use suitable biological control.
Blossom End Rot
Dark leathery patch at fruit base.
Keep root moisture even, especially as fruit swells.
SPLIT FRUIT
Skins crack after uneven watering.
Keep moisture steady; avoid drying then flooding.
Tomato Leaf Mould
Yellow patches above; brown mould below.
Remove infected leaves; ventilate and avoid wet foliage.
Aphids
Colonies gather on young growth.
Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones and favour predators.
Grey Mould (Botrytis)
Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.
Remove infected tissue; ventilate and clear dead material.
Blossom Drop
Flowers wither and fall without setting.
Water steadily, ventilate in heat and gently tap trusses.
Virus
Mottled, distorted leaves; stunted plants.
Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools and monitor aphids.
Magnesium Deficiency
Lower leaves yellow between green veins.
Check watering, pH and feed; avoid excess potash.
Check leaf undersides often so whitefly can be managed while numbers are still low.
Avoid high-potash overfeeding: balanced nutrition matters as much as the amount supplied.

DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5

Summer / Autumn

Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.

Harvest

Recommended varieties
CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sungold F1

A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.

ORDINARY
Alicante

A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.

F1 HYBRID
Shirley

An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.

CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sweet Million F1

A cordon tomato producing many small red cherry fruits. Complements orange Sungold with a familiar red-fruited alternative.

NOVELTY
San Marzano

A plum tomato for sauces and cooking. Give it warm protected conditions and distinguish it from fresh-eating cherry selections.

Key risks
BLIGHT

Tomato blight causes brown lesions on leaves and stems, followed by fruit decay and plant collapse in favourable damp conditions.

Greenhouse Whitefly

Whitefly adults and immature stages suck sap; sticky honeydew can support black sooty mould.

Blossom End Rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

SPLIT FRUIT

Irregular watering, particularly soaking after severe drying, can split ripe fruit.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

Growing guide · Tomato, Greenhouse
Water steadily and ventilate.

Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.

Train to the variety’s habit.

Remove side shoots from cordons; bush types need a different routine.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained border soil with compost, or suitable pots/growbags of fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale, humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding than a well-prepared border.
Looking after the crop
Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly; keep healthy leaves to feed and shade fruit. Stop two leaves above the final truss at the chosen height or near season’s end. Bush and semi-determinate pruning differs.
Water roots steadily; feed organically at the product rate as fruit develops. Ventilate in heat and gently tap flowering trusses. Match autumn watering to growth.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; use promptly. Before cold ends the crop, bring sound unripe fruit indoors. Ripen at room temperature, checking trays for decay; a nearby ripe apple or banana can help.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on in a pot

Sow in trays or small pots; keep compost moist, not wet. Prick out and pot on as needed. Bright light gives stout seedlings.

2 Plant and support

In a warm greenhouse, water well-rooted plants before setting slightly deeper in pots, growbags or beds. Support cordons with canes or string.

Pots / growbags One plant per 12–18 in. diameter pot; two per standard growbag. Use peat-free compost.
Pot spacing Upright cordons: about 24 in. between pot centres for foliage space.
Soil beds Plants 18–24 in. apart in compost-enriched soil; wider for vigorous cordons and airflow.

For unheated cover, sow around March in gentle warmth near 68°F. Earlier heated crops need reliable warmth and bright winter light.

Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
BLIGHT — Brown leaf lesions; fruit may rot.	Remove infected plants; keep leaves dry and ventilate.
Greenhouse Whitefly — White flies; sticky leaves and sooty mould.	Identify early; use suitable biological control.
Blossom End Rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
SPLIT FRUIT — Skins crack after uneven watering.	Keep moisture steady; avoid drying then flooding.
Tomato Leaf Mould — Yellow patches above; brown mould below.	Remove infected leaves; ventilate; keep foliage dry.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey Mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Blossom Drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Magnesium Deficiency — Lower leaves yellow between green veins.	Check watering, pH and feed; avoid excess potash.
Final tips

Check leaf undersides often; manage whitefly while numbers are low.

Avoid excess high-potash feed: nutrient balance matters as much as quantity.

fonts.text: Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.
Sow
Mar – Apr
Harvest
Jul – Oct
Germination
8–11 days
Yield per plant
4 lb
Plant spacing
Between plants: 18–24 in., allowing more room for vigorous plants
Ready in
About 20 weeks from sowing
Bright: usual months · Muted: less usual
Cordon
An early cordon tomato suited to outdoor growing. Provide support and remove sideshoots as for other cordon varieties.
Cordon
A familiar cordon tomato with small red fruits. A useful outdoor choice in a warm, sheltered position.
Cordon
A cordon tomato bred for outdoor growing with strong late-blight resistance. Produces large red fruits for slicing and cooking.
Cordon
A sweet orange cherry tomato for a sunny, sheltered outdoor site. Grow as a supported cordon and pick ripe fruits promptly.
Bush
An early bush tomato with small red fruits. Useful where compact plants are preferred to tall, trained cordons.
Blight causes rapidly spreading brown leaf and stem lesions and fruit decay in damp weather.
A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.
Slugs chew low-hanging fruit, particularly on bush plants.
Ripe fruit may split after irregular watering or rain following dry soil.
Early cropping and a warm, sheltered site improve the chance of ripe fruit.
Dry-to-wet swings split fruit and can encourage blossom-end rot.
Use fertile, well-drained soil enriched with mature compost in a sunny, sheltered spot. Improve heavy clay well before planting.
Pots and growing bags suit patios or limited space, but need frequent watering and regular organic feeding.
Raise seedlings under cover in spring or buy sturdy pot-grown plants. Harden them off gradually before outdoor planting.
Plant after frost risk in settled warm weather. Water first, preserve the rootball and set slightly deeper. Support tall types and tie in regularly.
Bush and basket types: follow packet spacing and support heavy stems; no routine side-shooting.
Sow under cover in March–early April. Harden off gradually and plant outside after frost risk in settled, warm late-spring weather.

Support cordons; add ties about every 12 in. and remove side shoots around 1 in. long. Stop above the final useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; retain healthy foliage. Bush types normally need no side-shooting or stopping.

Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Cloches reduce rain on leaves but need ventilation in warmth; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight and search beneath bush foliage for ripe or slug-damaged fruit.

Pick fully coloured fruit gently, keeping stalks where possible and avoiding skin damage; use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October, bushes July–September. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors at season’s end. Ripen in shallow trays at room temperature, checking for rot; a nearby ripe apple or banana helps. Use a tested recipe for bottling or green-tomato chutney.
Problem
What to look for
What to do
BLIGHT
Brown dying leaves; dark fruit rot.
Remove infected plants; keep foliage dry where practical.
Blossom End Rot
Dark leathery patch at fruit base.
Keep root moisture even, especially as fruit swells.
SLUGS
Low fruit is chewed or hollowed.
Keep fruit off soil; check and hand-pick around vulnerable plants.
SPLIT FRUIT
Fruit cracks after rain or uneven watering.
Keep root moisture steady and mulch.
Aphids
Colonies gather on young growth.
Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones and favour predators.
Grey Mould (Botrytis)
Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.
Remove infected tissue; ventilate and clear dead material.
Virus
Mottled, distorted leaves; stunted plants.
Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools and monitor aphids.
Blossom Drop
Flowers wither and fall without setting.
Water steadily, ventilate in heat and gently tap trusses.
CUTWORMS
Young stems are severed near soil level.
Protect seedlings with collars; inspect nearby soil.
Check hidden fruit on bush plants regularly: ripe tomatoes and slug damage are easily missed.
Stop tall plants in time for the local season; leave two leaves above the final truss.

Fruiting Crops
Tomato, Outdoor.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.

Recommended varieties
CORDON
Outdoor Girl

An early cordon tomato suited to outdoor growing. Provide support and remove sideshoots as for other cordon varieties.

CORDON
Gardener's Delight

A familiar cordon tomato with small red fruits. A useful outdoor choice in a warm, sheltered position.

CORDON
Crimson Crush F1

A cordon tomato bred for outdoor growing with strong late-blight resistance. Produces large red fruits for slicing and cooking.

CORDON
Sungold F1

A sweet orange cherry tomato for a sunny, sheltered outdoor site. Grow as a supported cordon and pick ripe fruits promptly.

BUSH
Red Alert

An early bush tomato with small red fruits. Useful where compact plants are preferred to tall, trained cordons.

Key risks
BLIGHT

Blight causes rapidly spreading brown leaf and stem lesions and fruit decay in damp weather.

Blossom End Rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

SLUGS

Slugs chew low-hanging fruit, particularly on bush plants.

SPLIT FRUIT

Ripe fruit may split after irregular watering or rain following dry soil.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
90

Growing guide · Tomato, Outdoor
Choose a suitable outdoor variety.

Early cropping and a warm, sheltered site improve the chance of ripe fruit.

Keep watering even.

Dry-to-wet swings split fruit and can encourage blossom-end rot.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained soil with mature compost in a sunny, sheltered spot. Improve heavy clay well before planting.
Pots/growbags suit patios or small spaces; water frequently and feed organically regularly.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on and harden

Raise seedlings under cover in spring or buy sturdy pot-grown plants. Harden off gradually before planting outside.

2 Plant beside support

After frost risk, plant in settled warmth. Water first; keep the rootball intact and set slightly deeper. Support tall types; tie in regularly.

Bush/basket types: use packet spacing; support heavy stems. No routine side-shooting.

Sow under cover in March–early April; plant outside in settled, warm late-spring weather after frost risk.

Looking after the crop
Support cordons; tie about every 30 cm and remove side shoots around 2.5 cm long. Stop above the last useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; keep healthy foliage. Bushes normally need no side-shooting or stopping.
Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Ventilate cloches in warmth: they reduce rain on leaves; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; keep stalks where possible, avoid skin damage and use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October; bushes July–September. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors at season’s end. Ripen in shallow trays at room temperature; check for rot. A ripe apple or banana nearby helps. Use tested bottling or green-tomato chutney recipes.
Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
BLIGHT — Brown dying leaves; dark fruit rot.	Remove infected plants; keep foliage dry where practical.
Blossom End Rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
SLUGS — Low fruit is chewed or hollowed.	Keep fruit off soil; check and hand-pick near vulnerable plants.
SPLIT FRUIT — Fruit cracks after rain or uneven watering.	Keep root moisture steady and mulch.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey Mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Blossom Drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
CUTWORMS — Young stems are severed near soil level.	Protect seedlings with collars; inspect nearby soil.
Final tips

Check beneath bush foliage often: ripe fruit and slug damage are easily missed.

Stop tall plants in time for the local season; leave two leaves above the final truss.
